topic: Hilbert finishes a remark on the correct criterion for a definition, then plans to extend the principle of continued identities to permutation groups and to Kummer's theory of ideal numbers, and begins a remark comparing mathematicians to miners.

triage.modern_statement: This is too fragmentary to pin down for certain. The page context suggests Hilbert was asking what plays the role of the 'identities' when his 'principle of continued identities' is carried over to permutation groups and to Kummer's ideal numbers. A reasonable guess, which the sources do not confirm: 'identities' means the relations (syzygies) among invariants, and 'continued' identities means relations among relations, which is the setting of the syzygy theorem in Hilbert's 1890 paper. On that reading the question would be: what is the analogue of a syzygy chain, i.e. a finite free resolution, for permutation groups and for ideals in algebraic number fields? Modern homological algebra (group cohomology, resolutions over rings other than polynomial rings) covers that idea in general, but I found nothing linking this note to it.
triage.answered_by: Not identifiable. No source I found discusses this notebook entry or says what Hilbert meant by 'Identitäten' here. His published 1890 syzygy theorem handles continued relations only for polynomial rings and invariants.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's syzygy theorem, published in 'Über die Theorie der algebraischen Formen' (1890), is about relations (syzygies) among generators and about continuing to relations among relations until the process stops. This is the likely meaning of 'continued identities' in the invariant-theory setting.
Background on Kummer's ideal numbers, the second area Hilbert planned to apply the principle to. The source says nothing about the notebook.

triage.why: The note is a single short question with no technical content. My searches turned up no edition or secondary study of notebook 600_1 that explains the 'principle of continued identities' or this entry. The link to syzygies is my own interpretation from context, and no source confirms it. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. I can't say whether Hilbert or anyone else later answered this exact question.
